newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Sakakibara no stranger to controversy.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Sakakibara no stranger to controversy.

text.p: Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara is a rarity in Japan -- a nail that sticks up but has not been hammered down.

The controversial, outspoken Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr Yen" for his ability to sway currency markets with a single comment, faces a new challenge now he is poised for promotion to the post of Japan's foremost financial diplomat.

A Finance Ministry official told reporters on Friday that Sakakibara would take over on July 15 as vice finance minister for international affairs, a step up after two years as director-general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau.

The appointment was widely expected after speculation faded that his detractors might succeed in keeping Takatoshi Kato -- a soft-spoken man inclined to cautious comments -- as vice minister for an unusual third year.

Sakakibara has been credited with spearheading a drive to counter the yen's steep rise in 1995 with financial market liberalisation steps and was instrumental in revising foreign exchange laws as a step towards Tokyo's "Big Bang" reforms.
He also played a key role in forging pacts with Asian nations to stabilise regional currencies.
"Japan faced a real economic emergency (in spring 1995) when the yen was around 80 (to the dollar) and the stock market was falling," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan.
Sakakibara's aggressive personality and some alleged missteps in the past won him many enemies within the ministry, but the tide appears to have shifted since then.

"His support in the ministry is much more broad-based than two years ago. Then, he was odd man out for his controversial views and controversial ways of doing things. But success has proven him right," Koll said.
Sakakibara had already earned a reputation as a tough negotiator in U.S.-Japan talks on deregulation of Japan's insurance market when he took up his current post in June 1995.

A fluent English speaker who earned a doctorate at the University of Michigan after graduating from the prestigious University of Tokyo, Sakakibara's economic views also earned him a place among a circle of intellectuals and bureaucrats dubbed by some as "Japan's new nationalists".

Those views were laid out in his book "Beyond Capitalism", in which he argued that Japan has a distinctive non-capitalist market economy which might be a better guide for developing nations than the U.S. model. Japanese firms, he said, compete in more or less free markets but the system places people above profits and mere efficiency.

Despite his support for Japan's Big Bang reforms, which are aimed at introducing more competition into Japan's long-protected financial sector, Sakakibara insists Japan can cling to a core of traditional values.
"With regard to financial and information technology, we must catch up with Europe and the United States," he was quoted as saying in a magazine interview earlier this year.
"But it is quite possible to remain Japanese while incorporating these, and I think ultimately the Japanese spirit of cooperation and harmony is very important," he said.

Sakakibara's close ties with U.S. and Asian counterparts will be a plus in his new top post. His penchant for speaking out and standing up for his own views could also work to good effect, although his abrasive style might make it tough to forge consensus if it pushes opponents to dig in their heels.

"It would be good to have someone with a clear vision of where he wants to go," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia. "There are real decisions to be made and he's a guy who is not afraid to make them."
But Sakakibara's promotion could also bring more volatility to foreign exchange markets given his brashness.
"The higher up you go in the hierarchy the greater risk loquaciousness is," Feldman said.

Sakakibara will be succeeded at the International Finance Bureau by Haruhiko Kuroda, an expert in tax and budget matters, who is currently president of the ministry's Institute of Fiscal and Monetary Policy.
"His intellectual clout is spectacular and he is highly respected," Koll said of Kuroda. But he added: "I think he will be less vocal (than Sakakibara) and more of an inside-the-ministry player."
